title: Equal Sum Grid Partition II
statement:
Every cell of the `m x n` matrix `grid` holds a positive integer. Decide whether one straight cut, either between two neighbouring rows or between two neighbouring columns, can split it into two non-empty parts that balance:

- the two parts have the same sum, or
- they reach the same sum once a single cell is left out of one of the parts (at most one cell overall), provided the cells that remain in that part are still connected.

Connected means that any cell of the part can be reached from any other through a chain of side-by-side neighbours (up, down, left, right) that all belong to the part. Return `true` if some cut balances this way, otherwise `false`.
notes:
## Intuition

A brute force tries every cut and every cell to leave out, with a flood fill to test connectivity. Two facts make it fast. Each part is a rectangle: with at least 2 rows and 2 columns it stays connected without any one cell, but a single row or column stays connected only without one of its two ends. And as a cut moves down, the part above it grows by one row, so a running prefix sum gives both part sums, and a set of the values above the cut tells at once whether some cell is worth exactly the surplus. Values are positive, so the left-out cell comes from the heavier part.

## Approach

1. Add up every cell into `total`.
2. `check(matrix)` moves a cut down `matrix`: for the cut below the first `k` rows it adds row `k - 1` to `topSum` and its values to `seen`.
3. `diff = topSum - (total - topSum)` is the top part's surplus. 0 means the parts balance; a negative surplus is left to the upside-down pass.
4. Leave out a cell worth `diff`: any value in `seen` when the top part has at least 2 rows and 2 columns, only `matrix[0][0]` or `matrix[k - 1][0]` when it is one column, only `matrix[0][0]` or `matrix[0][cols - 1]` when it is one row.
5. Run `check` on `grid`, on `grid` upside down (the bottom part becomes the top), and likewise on `transposed` for the vertical cuts.

## Example 1, step by step

`grid = [[1, 4], [2, 3]]`, so `total = 10`. In `check(grid)` the cut with `k = 1` gives `topSum = 1 + 4 = 5` and `diff = 5 - 5 = 0`: the parts already balance, so the answer is `true`. (Example 2 is found by the upside-down pass: on `[[3, 4], [1, 2]]`, `diff = 7 - 3 = 4`, and 4 is the last cell of that one-row part.)

## Complexity

- Time: O(m·n): the total, the transpose and the four sweeps each visit every cell once.
- Space: O(m·n) for the flipped and transposed copies and `seen`.

## Pitfalls

- Leaving out a middle cell of a one-row or one-column part splits it (Example 3), even when the grid itself has many rows.
- The heavier part may lie on either side of a horizontal or vertical cut: check all four orientations.
- In a part with at least 2 rows and 2 columns any cell may go, inner ones included.
- Under LeetCode's limits sums reach 10^10; in Java or C use a 64-bit `long`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `total` | sum of all cells |
| `matrix` | the grid in the orientation being checked |
| `rows`, `cols` | its numbers of rows and columns |
| `k` | the cut lies below the first `k` rows |
| `topSum` | prefix sum of the rows above the cut |
| `seen` | set of the values above the cut |
| `diff` | how much heavier the top part is than the bottom part |
| `transposed` | the grid with rows and columns swapped, for vertical cuts |
